title: The Final Electric Days of Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate Campaign
author: @NewYorker
content:
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for Senate in Michigan, never had a bodyguard before this campaign. Now he has three. “When the President is constantly coming after you, there’s real consequences,” he told me. We were sitting in the back of his campaign bus, heading toward Caro, a rural town in the thumb of Michigan’s mitten. El-Sayed, slumped on a black leather bench, was keeping his gaze forward to avoid motion sickness. On his right wrist, El-Sayed wears a jumble of Taylor Swift-style beaded bracelets, and I asked him about one, which read, “FUCKING WOLVERINE.” He explained that, at a recent campaign stop in Michigan, Vice-President J. D. Vance had called him “a little weasel,” and added that he should “shut his mouth and show more gratitude to the country that gave him everything.” El-Sayed had twisted the barb and hurled it back. “Nobody understands how deep and profound the gift of this country is like a kid who was born here but for the accident of history that allowed that to happen,” he’d said. “J. D. Vance called me a little weasel today. I’m, like, ‘No, no, no. What you’re talking about is a fucking wolverine.’ ” A supporter made him the bracelet, and handed it to him at a recent campaign stop.

Hate has played an arresting role in the late stages of Michigan’s Senate race, in which El-Sayed is facing the former U.S. congressman and Donald Trump ally Mike Rogers. At a rally in Port Huron early this week, Trump announced, “I’m here to keep a jihadist Muslim Brotherhood member from becoming a U.S. senator.” In August, Vance said, “There’s something about Abdul El-Sayed that is very, very evil and on the rise in the United States of America today”; he claimed that El-Sayed sees himself “as fighting for one group at the expense of others.” El-Sayed replied, in part, by calling Vance a “sock puppet.” On the campaign bus, he told me, “Donald Trump and J. D. Vance, because they’re fools, built me one of the biggest and best platforms of any incoming United States senator.”

Many recent polls show El-Sayed leading Rogers by only a few points, within their margins of error. “You need every vote here,” El-Sayed’s wife, Sarah Jukaku, told me. “It’s not like California, which is a huge state but you can take things for granted a bit.” A little-known part of his strategy is to run up a lead on the Upper Peninsula, which is home to only three hundred thousand people, or three per cent of Michigan’s population. El-Sayed performed particularly well there in the primary—in which he lost Detroit and Flint to the establishment candidate Haley Stevens—and the latest figures from the Detroit News show that he continues to be a favorite there, putting him nearly six points ahead of Rogers in the U.P. and northern Michigan.

“If you want rural, working-class communities to be in play, you’ve got to come to the Upper Peninsula,” Chloe Kannan, a local organizer and a member of the Sault tribe, said. We met on a blustery afternoon at a protest that she was leading in the city of Sault Ste. Marie, outside a red brick local hospital that had been bought several years ago by a larger health-care provider. In the distance, a white double-humped steel bridge spanned the St. Marys River. Ontario was on the other side.

At the protest, two dozen locals, some in “Yoopers for Abdul” T-shirts, gathered around the open bed of a pickup truck. Kannan and others took turns standing in the bed, and recounting the firing of doctors and staff, until a white Grand Wagoneer pulled up and El-Sayed got out. He was dressed in his campaign uniform of a Carhartt jacket over a tight black T-shirt and dark-wash jeans, and accompanied by his three bodyguards. Climbing up into the truck bed alongside Kannan, he told the group, “The fight for this particular hospital is the fight for rural health care across the country.” El-Sayed, a doctor and the former director of Wayne County’s department of health and human services, is running on a double-barrelled slogan of “Money out of politics” and “Medicare for all,” and vying for voters disillusioned by the mainstream of both parties. There are “people locked out of the system and people doing the locking out,” he told me. “I’m for the people locked out.”

Since 2025, El-Sayed has made four trips to the Soo, as locals call Sault Ste. Marie, a rural outpost that for thousands of years has been a gathering place and trading hub for Indigenous communities. He’s entered Ojibwe sweat lodges twice, once at a local health center and a second time at a private home. I learned about his experience only through members of the Native community, who were moved by his commitment to working on behalf of the greater good. “He’s up against some very dark energy,” Lori Gambardella, a traditional-medicine supervisor, who’d conducted the sweat lodges that El-Sayed attended, told me. At the hospital rally, she hugged him before he spoke. Two Ojibwe elders, both women, said that they were so taken with El-Sayed that they’d given him a hand-crafted drum.“A hand-drum is the heartbeat of our people,” one of the women, Janet Liedel, told me. She worked as a cashier at a local supermarket and was registered as an independent; she was voting for the person, not the party.

El-Sayed was among the Michiganders exceedingly confident of his forthcoming victory. “I want to focus on governing,” he told me. He was already thinking about how to strike working relationships with Ted Cruz, among other opponents, to move his bid for universal health care forward. He was also looking forward to welcoming the two tribal women on their road trip to Washington, D.C., when they came to visit him and to see their drum.

El-Sayed’s reputation is that of a know-it-all who is happy to scorch anyone who opposes him. “Abdul isn’t short on confidence, and I know that can make people nervous if it comes across as arrogance,” the Michigan state senator Mallory McMorrow, who suspended a campaign for the Democratic nomination for the Senate, told me. “But if Abdul can convince people he’s listening to them and fighting for them, and not just asking them to fight for him, he can win this thing.” Jukaku, his wife, described him as a counterpuncher. “If you are respectful, he will be so respectful. If you are kind and warm, he will be so kind and warm. He will mirror it with more,” she told me. And, “if you’re going to be arrogant to him, he’s gonna be more.” El-Sayed gave me a similar account of his persona: “Bad-faith questions get bad-faith answers,” he said, after a dustup in Bay City with Fox News.

After his swing through the Upper Peninsula, El-Sayed had headed south, to the thumb of Michigan’s mitten. In Caro, after four long days on the bus, and with multiple stops per day, he bounded onstage, delivering his stump speech like a standup routine. “Donald Trump and J. D. Vance can’t seem to keep my name out of their mouth,” he’d said. “However they want to say it, we’re going to make sure they say it with the word ‘Senator’ in front in November.” El-Sayed invoked Bill Clinton, who’d urged him to run for public office after hearing him speak at his college graduation, at the University of Michigan, in 2007. He mentioned Barack Obama, too. The two had a lot in common, El-Sayed said. Not height. “He’s tall and skinny, and I’m”—he paused—“five-eight.” The crowd broke into warm, if expectant, laughter.

When the Q. & A. began, a twentysomething white man wearing a gray T-shirt with a rainbow sticker on it raised his hand. When called on, the man, who said his name was Tommy, asked El-Sayed, “Will you disavow the Muslim Brotherhood?” Claims that El-Sayed supports the Muslim Brotherhood have dogged his campaign, based on social-media posts that his half sister made in 2012, and a letter that he’d signed that year in support of Mohamed Morsi, then the President of Egypt and a former leader of the group. El-Sayed seemed prepared to escalate—“What are you implying?” he asked—but, as Tommy kept drilling the “simple” question, El-Sayed switched tacks. “Sure, yeah, but why are you asking the question?” he said to Tommy.

“I haven’t heard you disavow them yet,” Tommy said. “I haven’t heard you disavow them yet,” El-Sayed shot back, and the room burst into laughter. A five-minute civics lesson followed, in which El-Sayed schooled Tommy on the U.S. Constitution and the allegations of dual loyalty levelled against J.F.K., as the first Catholic President. “You assume, Tommy, because I’m Muslim that I would have some allegiance to something that’s not the U.S. Constitution,” El-Sayed said. He asked if Tommy, who’d called himself a Christian, honored the U.S. Constitution’s separation of church and state. Tommy demurred. (The clip soon went viral, and has been viewed fifty million times.)

When their exchange ended, I spotted Tommy making a beeline for the exit and followed him. In the parking lot, I asked if he was satisfied with El-Sayed’s answer. “Abdul said he did disavow the Muslim Brotherhood,” Tommy said. “I’ve seen him skirt around the question a lot, so to get a straight answer was satisfactory.” Did it change his opinion about El-Sayed? “Not so much,” he replied. A few minutes after Tommy left, two black sedans pulled out of the lot, with homemade signs on top that read, in red and blue marker, “MICHIGAN IS TOO AMERICAN FOR ABDUL.” When I texted Tommy later to ask if he was inside one of the sedans, he didn’t reply.

Tommy, it turned out, is Tommy Teepell, a political operative, and a former aide to Josh Hawley, the Missouri senator and avowed Christian nationalist. He is also the son of Timmy Teepell, a G.O.P. strategist, whose firm, Breakthrough L.L.C., received two hundred and fifty thousand dollars from America Next, a nonprofit waging a “war of ideas” on behalf of conservative America. According to F.E.C. filings, the payment was intended to fund opposition to El-Sayed through “influencer marketing.” America Next also appears to be backing stunts like Tommy’s: at the University of Michigan, a leaked chat among college Republicans revealed that a senior who claimed to be working for America Next offered students two hundred dollars to heckle El-Sayed at events.“We are going to coordinate questions to ask him and spread out to increase the chances we’re called on. We’re gonna boo him. We’re gonna show everyone that ABDUL IS NOT WELCOME IN THE SENATE,” the senior’s message read. (America Next did not respond to a request for comment.)

Jeff Timmer, a prominent Republican strategist in Michigan, told me, “The sad truth is that peddling fearmongering, hate, racism, and bigotry still works. It’s what Trumpism is built on, and it has replaced all pretense of traditional G.O.P. ideology.” Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate, has embraced the strategy, claiming, without offering any evidence, that El-Sayed has accepted campaign contributions from supporters of Hezbollah and Hamas. At the same time, race-baiting is, to some liberals, an indication that Republicans know they’re in trouble. “ ‘Let’s be racist’ strategy is not a strategy aimed at the middle or the left,” Hugh Madden, a strategist who has worked with labor unions and lives in the Upper Peninsula, said. “It suggests that Republicans have a base-turnout problem.”

Last weekend, Obama appeared with El-Sayed at Detroit’s Cass Technical High School. Onstage, the former President invoked the fact that he’d faced similarly hateful attacks. “They will use lies and maybe your name or your faith to somehow suggest you are dangerous and less than trustworthy and less patriotic and less American than they are,” he said. “This stuff didn’t work on me, not in Michigan. It’s not going to work on Abdul. Abdul is as Michigan as it gets.” Afterward, El-Sayed told me that he found it “pretty surreal to have the person who was the President of your twenties campaigning for you.” He was most moved, however, by the moments when Obama, a fellow “girl dad,” interacted with El-Sayed’s daughters, and “the grandfatherly way he did it.”

Obama’s presence in Detroit reflected a real area of concern for El-Sayed’s campaign. In the primary, he lost the city to Stevens, the moderate, by more than thirty points. There is, too, a recent history of pain and distrust between Detroit’s Black and Arab communities: in 2024, Arab voters, many of whom had joined the Uncommitted Movement to signal their disgust with Democrats over the war in Gaza, did not turn out in large numbers for Kamala Harris, and she lost the state. “It was a system-wide failure,” Abbas Alawieh, a co-founder of the Uncommitted Movement and a candidate for the state senate, told me over breakfast at a Lebanese restaurant in suburban Detroit. “You lost every single swing state.” But, he acknowledged, the political tensions between the two communities remained. “It’s a huge concern,” Alawieh said.

“People are torn,” Karen Weaver, the former mayor of Flint, told me. She herself supports El-Sayed. “I’m anti-establishment, and that’s what I like,” she said. But Weaver, who sits on the leadership committee of the state chapter of Win with Black Women, a network of Black women leaders, said that the message from some of her peers was, “When we needed you, you didn’t have our back.” She went on, “And Black women vote. We’re loyal, and we vote.” Weaver, among others, wasn’t sure how this resentment would play out at the ballot box.

One Sunday last month, El-Sayed, along with the Massachusetts congresswoman Ayanna Pressley, visited Metropolitan Baptist Tabernacle, in Flint, Michigan, where he clapped in the pews and told the story of his grandmother, who raised eight children in poverty in Egypt, losing two in childhood. It was the church’s “Survivor” Sunday: breast-cancer survivors wore pink; domestic-violence survivors purple. Before the service began, a congregant named Anita Harris ushered people to their seats. “They’re trying to get Black people not to vote for him because of Harris,” she told me. She also kept seeing ads that cast him as a terrorist. “I don’t think that Black people feel that stuff is true,” she said. Harris, a retiree, explained that she had worked for General Motors all her life: “When the United Auto Workers endorsed him, that’s good enough for me.”

El-Sayed’s connection with Michigan’s Jewish population has been similarly strained. El-Sayed has said that he does not view Israel as an American ally and that he rejects its existence as a Jewish state. Recently, a debate moderator asked El-Sayed whether Israel or Iran posed a greater threat to the U.S., he refused to answer, calling it “a ridiculous question.” Jordan Acker, a member of the University of Michigan Board of Regents and a former Obama Administration official, told me, “My issue with him isn’t about Israel policy. It’s the way he speaks about Jews.” He was unsettled by El-Sayed’s frequent implication that, because the U.S. government sends aid to Israel, it’s not providing Americans with adequate health care. And he took note when, after an attacker opened fire at West Bloomfield Township’s Temple Israel, in March, forcing the evacuation of more than a hundred preschoolers, El-Sayed said, “Hurt people hurt people.” (He has since apologized for the phrase, which was part of a longer condemnation of the attack.)

In a recently released campaign ad, El-Sayed tries to distinguish between his affection for the Jewish people and their faith and his disdain for the “foreign government” of Israel. To Acker, this solved nothing. “Abdul is deeply thoughtful, deeply charming, very smart, and a great speaker,” he said. “He stands for ninety-five per cent of my values, but the most basic value we have is inclusion.” To him, a question remained unanswered: Do people who believe in the state of Israel have a place in El-Sayed’s Democratic Party? Acker continued, “My top issue is the safety of my children, and nothing I’ve heard from the El-Sayed campaign suggests they take that seriously at all.” He was still undecided about his vote.

El-Sayed has tried to reassure Jewish voters, saying, in August, “My commitment to Jewish safety is the same commitment that I have to the safety of my own daughters.” He added, “We can be talking about antisemitism and at the same time we can be talking about how we bring people together. And we can be talking about everybody’s pain. And I think that anybody who does not want to do that is not serious about actually addressing the hurt that we see across the board.”

On the campaign bus, I noticed one bracelet tucked beneath the others. It read “BEST DAD.” When I asked El-Sayed about it, his throat caught. His two daughters had made it for him. He began to cry. He missed them, and his wife, Sarah, and he also worried that his choice to run for office had put them in danger. He said the F.B.I. had recently alerted local law enforcement to a threat against him, and he hadn’t had a chance to tell his wife before she allowed the two girls to head, on their own, to a friend’s house down the street. He continued, “I’ll be honest, I’ve had a recurring dream that I’m going to get—I’m going to die young, my whole life.” The tactics being levelled against him weren’t new, he noted. “This has always been the play.” ♦

title: Uncertainty in Israel After Election Results
author: @NewYorker
content:
As the projected results of Israel’s elections were announced on Tuesday night, the atmosphere in Tel Aviv was oddly quiet. In Habima Square, which has hosted raucous anti-government protests in the past three years, only a trickle of people showed up. Some waved the Israeli flag, colored pink to signify resistance; others walked around in a daze. No one seemed to know whether to celebrate or weep.

Here’s what the results showed: A decisive majority of Israelis rejected the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. His coalition of far-right and ultra-Orthodox partners went into the election with sixty-eight seats, out of a hundred and twenty; it is projected to emerge with fifty-three—eight seats short of what Netanyahu needs to form a majority government.

Palestinian citizens of Israel voted in unprecedented numbers, with a turnout rate estimated as high as eighty per cent. Predominantly Arab parties are projected to have almost doubled their representation in the Knesset, from ten to nineteen seats. It’s not hard to imagine that the current political climate would discourage Palestinian Israelis from voting: the national-security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, openly regards them as enemies; gangs of Jewish settlers act with impunity in the West Bank; Gaza has been almost completely destroyed. Instead, their outrage seemed to have served as an extraordinary mobilizer. Many of them were reportedly inspired to vote by Ben-Gvir’s claim that he would demand the defense ministry in the next government.

But the results also show that Netanyahu’s Likud Party maintained its dominance. His main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, fell short of the results that most polls predicted. Eisenkot’s party, Yashar, is projected to have twenty-one seats—a decent showing for a new party, but not a groundswell by any measure.

If you combine the Jewish parties and the Arab parties in the anti-Netanyahu bloc, they secured more votes. But the pro-Netanyahu bloc won more votes from Jewish Israelis. Many will view this as the election’s bottom line: that a “Zionist majority” is the only one that counts. (What they mean is a Jewish majority. The ultra-Orthodox parties are openly anti-Zionist.) Eisenkot himself seems to have adopted a similar framework when the exit polls were first released. “Netanyahu finds himself tonight facing a larger and stronger Zionist majority,” he said.

“It is disappointing, but comes as no surprise,” Noa Landau wrote in the left-leaning newspaper Haaretz, to see how Eisenkot “framed the election results in the form of a ‘Zionist’ majority for a government led by him and fell precisely—and I mean, precisely––into the trap Netanyahu laid for him.”

Under the Israeli electoral system, the next step is for the country’s President, Isaac Herzog, to ask party leaders which candidate they recommend for Prime Minister. That candidate then has roughly a month to form a majority. As things stand, it is unclear whether that task will fall to Netanyahu, the leader of the largest party, or Eisenkot, who could become the leader of the largest bloc of parties. But Eisenkot would need support from Arab parties to form a coalition, and he spent his campaign equivocating on whether he would be willing to do so; some of his partners in the opposition have flatly rejected the idea.

That leaves Netanyahu. His campaign strategy in the days before the election seemed to rely on scaring the Israeli public into voting for him. In a series of interviews, Netanyahu acknowledged that the multi-billion-dollar annual defense package that the U.S. gives Israel “is over.” He added that crippling international sanctions were inevitable, so the country should be prepared to “circumvent” them by turning to cryptocurrency. (He seemed to regard his government’s policy of expanding Jewish settlements in the West Bank, which has already triggered sanctions from eleven European countries, as irreversible.) The comments rattled markets and scandalized experts. “All he has to offer the Israeli economy is a bizarre solution that is common among criminal organizations,” a scathing letter signed by more than a hundred Israeli economists concluded.

Netanyahu will now do everything in his power to peel lawmakers away from the opposition to cobble together a majority. It won’t be easy. Although some opposition leaders vowed not to sit in a coalition with Arab parties, all of them vowed not to join one headed by Netanyahu. This is the deadlock that many Israelis feared going into the election. It means that the country will now face weeks or months of coalition wrangling, of raw nerves and bitter infighting—only to risk ending up in the same impasse.

Once those negotiations are exhausted, there are two likely scenarios. There will be enormous pressure from within Israel and from abroad to form some sort of national-unity government, headed by both Netanyahu and Eisenkot. Trump indicated as much, when unnamed U.S. sources told Israeli media that he wants to “make sure” that the next government does not include Ben-Gvir. On Wednesday, the popular Israeli news site Ynet laid out a possible framework for such a government. It would include Netanyahu, Eisenkot, and Naftali Bennett—a former Prime Minister who is now in the opposition. The article suggested that the three would each take a turn serving as Prime Minister, in alignment with “Trump’s vision.”

For Netanyahu, though, breaking away from his longtime ultra-Orthodox partners could spell the beginning of his political end. (The last time he turned his back on them, in 2013, his coalition splintered after less than two years.) Eisenkot and Bennett also seem unlikely to agree to a unity government anytime soon. Not only did they promise voters that they would not join forces with Netanyahu—they also personally believe that he represents an active danger to democracy. “I know Netanyahu,” Eisenkot said on a recent campaign stop, in Tel Aviv. “He’ll stop at nothing” to remain in power. Bennett, for his part, has called Netanyahu’s aides’ alleged work as influence agents for Qatar the “most serious act of treason” in the country’s history. Yet they might reconsider if Israel seemed headed toward another imminent escalation with Iran. On Wednesday, the Wall Street Journal reported that the U.S. and Israel were preparing for a possible round of strikes on Iran after the American midterms.

The other scenario is that the results will be so inconclusive that, in a few months, Israelis will be sent to the ballot box again. It wouldn’t be the first time. Between 2019 and 2021, there were four rounds of elections in just two years, and the government that was ultimately sworn in dissolved within eighteen months.

Netanyahu may well be counting on a repeat election. He knows that Israelis living abroad, an estimated sixty-seven thousand of whom showed up to vote in this week’s elections, are unlikely to make another trip in a few short months. And Arab Israelis are unlikely to repeat their historic turnout if they conclude that it did nothing to improve their standing. In that scenario, Netanyahu would not only stay in office, as the leader of a caretaker government; he could emerge from the next election with a wider lead and a solidified base of support.

Eisenkot is clearly aware of that risk. Early on Wednesday, he said that, after an election “with such high turnout,” it would be “a mistake” to call another.

And so, in opposition circles and in online forums, momentum began gathering around a simple argument. The anti-Netanyahu bloc, along with the Arab parties, will have a decisive majority in the next parliament. Why not use it?

“We can no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” Yair Golan, who heads a left-wing opposition party called the Democrats, wrote as results filtered in. Golan is the only Jewish party leader who had stated that he would happily join a coalition with an Arab party. He added, “The vote of an Israeli citizen voting in Tira”—an Arab city—“is worth exactly the same as that of an Israeli citizen voting in Givat Shmuel,” a Jewish city. Historically, it’s not only that Arab parties were excluded from coalition negotiations. They themselves refused to participate, so as not to be seen as aiding the Zionist project. That changed in 2021, when Mansour Abbas, the head of an Islamist party called Ra’am, joined Bennett’s short-lived government.

Amit Segal, a political commentator for Channel 12 who is deeply influential on the right, on Tuesday tried to brush off Arab voters’ electoral potential. “The Israeli government will not sing ‘Biladi, Biladi,’ ” he said, referring to the Egyptian national anthem, which one Arab-majority alliance had reportedly sung as returns came in.

The Arab Israeli vote is largely divided between two parties: the Joint List, an alliance of factions which is projected to have twelve seats, and Ra’am, which is projected to have seven. Abbas had already proved willing to be an active member in a coalition government. Yousef Jabareen, the leader of the Joint List, expressed the same willingness on Wednesday. Jabareen said that he was prepared to “leverage our political power to advance the values we believe in.” He put forth a stark choice before the Israeli people. “It is either continued racism, continued exclusion, and continued supremacy, or genuine Jewish-Arab partnership,” he said. “We will be ready to pave the way to topple the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir, and Smotrich—and send them home.” ♦

title: The Unclassifiable Talent of Hervé Guibert
author: @NewYorker
content:
The French writer and photographer’s portraits of love.

October 27, 2026

Hervé Guibert’s ultimately unclassifiable talent brilliantly evokes the shadows, the moments of dread and paranoia, that are part of the experience of love. Doom lurks everywhere in Guibert’s world, in large part because love, as Guibert expresses it, is synonymous with longing, and what is longing but a pit stop on the way to hurt, loss, and the lover’s need to control the beloved?

Born in 1955, into a middle-class family in a suburb of Paris, Guibert, who wrote about photography in addition to taking pictures himself—he also published more than two dozen books of fiction, autofiction, and essays—was a gay man who came of age during the AIDS epidemic, a time of incalculable devastation. Guibert describes the epoch with what feels like a preternatural calm in his now classic 1990 novel, “To the Friend Who Did Not Save My Life,” in which we meet some of his friends, thinly disguised, including the philosopher Michel Foucault and the actress Isabelle Adjani. I remember reading about the book when it came out in the U.S. the following year—the year that Guibert died, at age thirty-six, of AIDS-related causes. Some people condemned the work for outing Foucault as a fellow AIDS sufferer. What right did Guibert have to tell someone else’s story? At some point, I read the book, and then I put the memory of reading it away: it was too potent, too sharp a reminder of what I had experienced during those years when quick and slow disasters were all around, and I felt ashamed of my helplessness and relative good health.

But then, about a decade ago, the writers Bruce Hainley and Jennifer Krasinski told me about a video that Guibert had made some months before his death. Titled “Modesty, or Immodesty” (1991), the hour-length work, shot by Guibert himself between June, 1990, and March, 1991, shows the artist going about his daily life in his final months, writing, talking on the phone, bathing, exercising, undergoing a medical procedure, then playing back the footage so that he can witness it, taking a holiday, and finally typing on a word processor, which continues to produce his text after he has moved on. This piece, Guibert’s single work on video, is an extraordinary film of self-dramatization: life and illness as a form of theatre. It is not a brave work—that’s too paltry a word for it. It is a powerful record of the isolating effects of AIDS, and of a patient who is running out of time and holding onto the act of creation as evidence that he has lived. As with “To the Friend Who Did Not Save My Life,” I did not want to remember the film after I had seen it; its solitude spoke of universal solitude, all those rooms filled with lost potential and the memory of the dead.

So it was with some trepidation, but also curiosity and not a little excitement, that I began looking at the volumes of Guibert’s photographs that were published recently, in elegant editions, by the Magic Hour Press. “The Only Face” is a version of the catalogue for a show that Guibert had in Paris, in 1984. The images are in black-and-white, and are romantic in a way that reminds one almost immediately of the photographer Duane Michals, another artist who worked with image and text. In the introduction to the original catalogue, Guibert wrote:

In writing, I have no brakes, no scruples, because I’m the only one, essentially, who’s at play (the others are relegated, as abstractions, to initials), whereas in photography, there are other people’s bodies, parents, friends, and I’m always a little apprehensive: aren’t I betraying them by turning them into visual objects in this way? That question, fortunately, is quickly dispelled by a second notion: that by revealing familiar bodies, beloved bodies, to strangers, bystanders who would quite possibly be indifferent (I can also imagine them being complicit), I’m doing only one thing—and it’s an enormous thing, I think, which is, in the end, the purpose of all my work, of all of my creative pretensions: to bear witness to my love.

Love doesn’t necessarily make a good photograph, but the photographer’s interest, and the intelligence and imagination behind it, can contribute to the making of a picture that interests us. It’s important to remember that Guibert was a very young man when he was taking these photographs, because sometimes the romanticism of his vision draws out a kind of artificiality that feels distinctly Gallic in its love of surface beauty; one longs to go deeper, to be allowed to go deeper, into the image.

The photographs are titled—“The mother,” “The father,” and so on—and the dominant visual theme in the work is the photographer’s fascination with the play of light in black-and-white. Too often Guibert goes for mood, as in “The fiancé” and “Sienna.” In the former, we see a figure shot from the front, draped in tulle. At first it’s not clear what sex the person is, but, looking closer, you can make out black hair across his chest. It’s a self-conscious study in texture, the kind of Photography 101 assignment you’re proud of yourself for having carried to completion, but Guibert’s lyricism topples over into kitsch in “Sienna.” In that picture, we see light pouring through a window. There’s smoke in the light. Is it cigarette smoke, or angels’ breath? A thin, shirtless figure sits in a chair with arms and head bent over a table. Again, it’s not a photograph but an image about photography, and Guibert’s too-romantic love of it.

Guibert’s love of Michals-influenced gay narrative also plays out in a piece called “The friend.” A white male hand rests on a broad, darker-skinned chest. That is all we see, in medium closeup, and the contrasts are obvious—light and dark, older and younger—but the picture stops there; what we are meant to register is not so much the bodies, their stories, as the photographer in the act of becoming one. (Helmut Newton is another influence. In Guibert’s portrait “Agathe,” a wavy-haired young woman looks out at us, her open jacket exposing her small breasts.)

Sometimes, though, Guibert is helped by a subject who works with him to make an emotionally legible picture that succeeds graphically as well. I don’t think I’ll soon forget his terrific portrait “Isabelle,” in which we see Adjani lying on a bench, her face turned to the camera. She wears a light-colored garment; her right arm rests on her belly. Adjani’s dark hair, the openness of her gaze, feels less like a study in grays and blacks than like a photograph about stillness. You can see how in their time together, the time it took to take this picture, Guibert was able to move past his love of the art of photography to the point of understanding it as an instrument of connection.

Like Adjani, the subjects of Guibert’s brilliant book “Suzanne and Louise” are so extraordinary that you can’t look away from them, and neither can the artist. Guibert called this book, originally published in France in 1980 and now available in English for the first time, a photo-novel, and that’s fine, but the category seems too limiting for what “Suzanne and Louise” is: a work as great as Jean Genet’s “The Maids,” and just as chilling. We’re in another black-and-white world, this time in a hôtel particulier in the Fifteenth Arrondissement, where two sisters, Suzanne and Louise, have lived for more than forty years. The fairly reclusive ladies, Guibert’s great-aunts, have had different lives: Louise was a Carmelite nun until she was convinced to leave the order by Suzanne, a widow who was once married to a pharmacist. Suzanne has money, and Louise does not. They share a dog named Whysky, and a marriage of sorts: Suzanne is the dominant figure, and Louise her poor relation who waits on her. The prose in the book is written from the inside; when Guibert was a child, he and his family made weekly visits to these sisters, who ultimately fascinated him enough that he was able to sidestep his overly aestheticized sensibility and let these singular beings speak and act and be in ways that are constantly startling and new. “Five years ago, I proposed to my great-aunts that I make a film about them; I had started writing a script, but their refusals were so categorical that I lost of [sic] all hope of ever making it,” Guibert writes. He was able to take photographs, though, and, as the contact sheets piled up, he decided to print some of the images, “just to see, to show them.” In a book of astonishing acts of intimacy, the most revealing is in a series of pictures that Guibert shot of Louise taking down her hair—her “most intimate thing.” Long ago, a woman would send a missed loved one a photograph of herself taking her hair down. In this case, Louise’s washing of her long gray tresses is less an erotic image than an act of self-dramatization in the theatre of being. It’s not a statement so much as a reckoning, a way of showing love to the young relative behind the camera who refuses to let these women not be in the world and then leave it, forgotten. ♦

title: Ghosts of the Grove
author: Krista Stevens
content:
Palmeros harvest medjool dates by hand by leaping into the crown of a tree “full of thorns sharp enough to puncture a tire—or, say, a human limb.” For Offrange, Ashley Stimpson introduces us to the workers who carry on a proud, 6,000-year-old farming tradition that’s in danger of dying out, just as date sales take off in the United States. (Photos by Siri Kaur.)

As far as harrowing job descriptions go, the palmero is up there with trapeze artist and surgeon. Must like heights, must work well in punishing heat, must feel comfortable yielding lethally sharp hand tools. In addition to brute labor, the job also requires an aptitude for botanical minutiae: the pungency of a ripening spadix, the dusky translucency of a perfectly ready date.

Palmeros spend most of their year in the top of the palm trees, which are dioecious plants, meaning male and female reproductive organs grow on separate trees. While the wind can carry pollen from tree to tree, it results in an unpredictable and uneven yield. Around 4000 BC in the Persian Gulf, our ancestors got wise and started cultivating the date palm by hand, kicking off a tradition Medina and Patino still carry out today.

More picks by Ashley Stimpson

“Creamer wasn’t just coming up against locals’ attachment to their horses, but a pernicious human tendency to confuse profound affection for animals with wisdom about what’s best for them.”

The Many Ways Scientists are Turning Birds into Feathered Field Assistants

“From frigatebirds and gulls to curlews and cormorants, researchers are tapping the ”Internet of Animals” to map, understand, and protect our changing world.”

title: Hot Wax sets fire to the Tetris playbook with slow-burn puzzle mechanics and a dollop of eldritch menace
author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
content:
Wicked

Over the past couple of weeks, I've been conscious of an eerie background humming and hissing. For a while I thought it was just tinnitus, brought on by one too many listens of Control's Ashtray Maze OST, but then I realised that it was actually RPS regular quasiotter whispering in my ear about Hot Wax, which launches on Steam this week after a spell of Itch.io exclusivity.

It's the new arcade puzzler from PUNKCAKE Délicieux, otherwise known for inflicting shotguns on chess and forcing the alphabet to wear trousers in the name of archaeology, somehow. Hot Wax is actually quite straightforward by PUNKCAKE standards. It's Tetris, but all the blocks are candles, and rather than filling a line on the grid to clear blocks, you have to plant unpredictably dropped flames on wicks to slowly sizzle the mass away. Relatively straightforward, yes, but fiddly in practice. Did I mention that you're doing all this in a temple, under the eye of a "not unfriendly" eldritch god?

There's still a demo for Hot Wax on Steam, with the full release due in Valve's cathedral of commerce tomorrow. I've had a go at that demo, and it has tickled my brain. You need to line up candles, wick to wick, rather than just filling gaps, as in Tetris. But you still, ideally, need to avoid gaps to slow down the filling of the screen. Once a wick is lit, it'll gradually melt the candle and leap to any other wicks it touches.

Once a candle is lit, you have to avoid smothering it by unscientifically dunking another candle on top of it, while trying to take advantage of how the melting wax alters the layout. I found this enjoyably challenging. And then there are the power-up items, acquired by sacrificing flames to the aforesaid "not unfriendly" god. These include bombs that light a bunch of wicks at once, and acorns that sprout a column-filling sapling. Not sure what they worship in this temple, exactly, other than Tetris.

There will be a bunch of modes in the full release – from basic score attack and endless play, to a mode where you have to melt several, painstakingly arranged candles with just one flame. They're also planning daily seeded challenge runs. As with PUNKCAKE stuff at large, it's a looker, with some lustrous pixel art and lots of nifty little animations. Thank you, quasiotter – this was fun! You can stop going "EEEEEEEE" in my ear now.

title: Benchma(r)king
author: Cheri Lucas Rowlands
content:
For Emergence Magazine, James Bridle writes about artificial intelligence; carpentry and chair-making with ChatGPT; and Enzo Mari, a famed Italian furniture designer from the 1950s and ’60s. Bridle asks: “What if we used AI for something actually useful?” They offer an interesting take on AI, and why the extractive way we’re using it is far from satisfying.

What we have here is, quite literally, a chair designed by someone who has read a lot about chairs but never actually sat in one. They know what a chair should look like, what it should do, the mechanics of how one is put together, the physics of holding you up. But they have no embodied experience of the world, no history with chairs or any other object, no physical memory. They don’t know how it feels, not merely to sit in a chair, but to encounter one in the world, to place it among other things in a home, to live with it, to be around it every day as one goes about the mundane business of life. This is the idea of a chair brought to life; but things—objects, beings, relationships—are not mere ideas, and you certainly can’t get every aspect of them from books. The chair is low stakes, but, once again, you wouldn’t want to run a society, or a culture, or a planet this way.

title: A Global Anti-Right Backlash
author: @NewYorker
content:
On a hazy Monday morning in Chandigarh, a city in northern India, Anish Gawande woke up early to check the news he had fallen asleep waiting for. Some nine thousand miles and eight time zones away, Brazil’s President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, had emerged the winner of his country’s Presidential runoff, a victory that two weeks earlier had seemed improbable. But the left-wing incumbent defied the polls and the prediction markets, mounted a campaign that turned tens of thousands out into the streets, mobilized countless more through social-media apps, and pulled in millions of voters who had not cast their ballot for him in the first round, earlier in the month. Lula’s comeback was inspiring to Gawande, a national spokesperson of one of India’s opposition parties and a voluble critic, on the evening news shows and social media, of the right-wing Hindu-nationalist government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi. In 2020, Gawande had protested the Modi government’s hosting of Brazil’s then President, Jair Bolsonaro—the convicted coup-plotting father of Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right challenger whom Lula defeated Sunday—as India’s chief guest for its annual Republic Day commemorations. Bolsonaro’s documented homophobia and his acceleration of the deforestation of the Amazon rain forest seemed, to Gawande, an echo of the divisive, destructive politics of Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party.

In recent months, Gawande has supported and defended the Gen Z uprising that has rocked Modi’s rule, with authorities unable to stamp out rolling protests in New Delhi and other Indian cities. The mass demonstrations, Gawande told me, have “revived the space for dissent in the country,” amid widespread anger over both an economy that has failed to create enough jobs for India’s huge population of young people and an increasingly autocratic politics where more than a hundred and thirty million people have been knocked off voter rolls on dubious grounds. Gawande saw a lesson in Lula’s ability to rally a diverse coalition of movements and parties in the perceived defense of Brazilian democracy. “What Lula’s victory demonstrates is that perhaps it is possible to craft solidarities between these movements, to assemble a rainbow coalition that can take on the might of Modi’s B.J.P.,” Gawande told me. He posted on Instagram, “If it happened in Brazil, it can happen in India.”

In this optimism, Gawande was joined by politicians far afield. After years of gloom in the shadow of President Donald Trump, Modi, Bolsonaro, and others of their ilk, progressives and liberals around the world are finding cause to celebrate. The center-left Spanish Prime Minister, Pedro Sánchez, who has called a snap election in the coming weeks against an emboldened right, declared, “What has happened in Brazil will happen in Spain,” adding, “The comeback of global progressivism has just begun.” Dominique de Villepin, a former French Prime Minister, said that Lula’s victory is “a major signal of hope,” even for France, where the far right is favored to win power in the Presidential elections next year, and where mass protests continue around the country. “The democrats have won the first round of a grand global referendum on democracy,” he wrote on X about Lula’s win.

Like the triumphalism of many from the West’s far right in earlier election cycles, such enthusiasm may be short-lived, a moment of transcendence soon to be subsumed by the churn of polarization and the sclerosis of daily politics. Sánchez’s plans on keeping his job hinge on, at best, cobbling together enough votes to form a stronger coalition than the minority government he currently leads. In India, the B.J.P. retains outsized control over the apparatus of state, the media, and the courts. In Brazil, inflation is high and public debt is surging, and the legislature and state governments are dominated by Lula’s opponents. But his win has blocked what seemed an inexorable advance of the right across Latin America, where left-leaning governments have fallen in rapid succession over the past two years, and has thwarted the Bolsonaros’ broader project of judicial overhaul at home and the potential yoking of Brazil’s foreign policy to Trump’s hemispheric agenda. Ahead of the runoff, Lula cast himself as the defender of Brazilian sovereignty from the predations of Washington and U.S. tech giants, and as the ally of working people against callous élites—he didn’t shy away from his own brand of populism. In the election’s aftermath, Bolsonaro briefly attempted to claim that the result was illegitimate, but he saw right-wing heads of state in South America recognize Lula’s victory. On Wednesday, Bolsonaro, who is under investigation for corruption, money laundering, and tax evasion, for accepting millions of dollars from a disgraced financier to produce a movie about his father, landed in Miami after fleeing Brazil. (Bolsonaro has not been formally charged and has denied any wrongdoing.)

Between the defeat of Bolsonaro this past week and events earlier this year in Hungary, where the long-ruling nationalist Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was ousted in elections, the White House has lost two hugely symbolic allies in its broader right-wing global culture war. By Wednesday, no clear winner had emerged in the Israeli election, in which Trump had endorsed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and which saw a historic turnout of Arab voters. And the U.S. President may be humbled further in next week’s midterms, as Democrats eye taking both the House and the Senate. Former President Barack Obama, while stumping for Democrats in Ohio, blasted the Republicans in terms that would have been familiar in Brazil and elsewhere, pointing to the wealthy élites and tech titans who “are able to buy and sell elections like never before,” in service of a Republican Party that “now seems to stand for corrupt government, or inept government, or no government.”

Lula withstood an anti-incumbency challenge on the same day that another once indomitable leader succumbed to one. The Serbian President, Aleksandar Vučić, a close Orbán ally, an erstwhile friend of the Kremlin, and a right-wing strongman effectively in power since 2012, saw his bid to stay in office by running to be Prime Minister foiled by an upstart student movement. The slate of candidates from its de-facto party, called the Student List, outperformed Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party, and he conceded. The students had been protesting since 2024, when the deadly collapse of a canopy outside a train station in the city of Novi Sad triggered a revolt over perceived state corruption and mismanagement. The protests, which were met at times with sweeping police repression, were resilient, and morphed into a strategic political project that persevered in the face of Vučić’s tactics, which included using state-media channels to tar the students as foreign stooges abetting a deep-state globalist agenda. Now they are trying to figure out how to form the next government in Belgrade, and, like Orbán’s opponents in Hungary, they have embarked on a campaign to reinforce the rule of law in the country and to purge state institutions of those who enabled their autocratic capture.

Those efforts are being mirrored elsewhere. “The vision of Serbian youth converges with that of many other young Europeans,” Nathalie Tocci, an Italian political scientist and former foreign-policy adviser to top E.U. officials, wrote in La Stampa. She pointed to the series of protests convulsing the Continent: there’s the Flamingo movement in Albania—where demonstrations have pulled in a cross-section of society, including students and professionals, infuriated by the government’s handling of a project backed by Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner to open a luxury resort along a coastal ecological preserve, and have surfaced wider public rage against oligarchs in the country. And then there are those who have marched in recent weeks in France, Belgium, Spain, and Italy, calling for access to affordable housing, relief with the cost of living, and greater investment in their schools. “It is a vision of democracy, equality, and social, environmental, international, and intergenerational justice,” Tocci added. “A vision and a commitment expressed through street protests.”

Of course, that’s not the universal view of the unrest. In the chaotic recent scenes from Paris and other French cities, in particular, members of the American and European right have sought confirmation for their culture-war talking points, laying the blame for the vandalism, fires on the boulevards, and looting on Muslim migrants and the alleged leftist extremists who appease them. Online, some Republicans and their supporters linked the chaos to the supposedly globalist world view of Democrats, invoking the spectral menace of communists and jihadists storming through the West’s fallen capitals. But that hysteria misses deeper realities, including the entrenched traditions of confrontational protest in France.

Political Islam has nothing to do with these protests. The unrest began with students unhappy about conditions in their schools and universities, but ballooned into something far larger, activating a swathe of French society that reviles the perceived neoliberalism of President Emmanuel Macron and wants to see greater public investment. It also pulled in apolitical opportunists who participated in the looting, while the government blamed the “ultra left.” Like the Gen Z protests in New Delhi earlier this summer, the protests, which were largely peaceful, were met at times with a crushing police response. Yet some observers have warned that the actions of a minority of the crowd—ransacking businesses and an arson attack that gutted the town hall of Limoges—may be strengthening the hand of the far-right leader Marine Le Pen. Macron is profoundly unpopular, complicating the path for a centrist successor next year. The protesters see their revolutionary zeal as offering a kind of renewal to a flagging French republic—one of their slogans is “On refait 1789 pour ne pas revenir en 1939,” that is, “We are redoing 1789 so as not to return to 1939.” Whether a majority of French voters will be persuaded by the spectacle of the barricades remains to be seen.

There’s no simple narrative bringing together all the separate uprisings. “They are dispersed points of resonance that still need to be tuned to one another,” the Belgian philosopher Michel Feher told an interviewer. Sánchez, in Spain, called the snap election when his ruling coalition was unable to pass housing legislation that many Spaniards had been demanding. In India, anger over the administration of school-board exams snowballed into a larger rebellion against Modi’s illiberal, majoritarian rule. But Matthew Cebul, a researcher on nonviolent resistance movements at the Harvard Kennedy School, sees all these protests as rooted in a universal desire for accountability from one’s government and rage at perceived graft and cronyism. “Illiberal governments thrive on this aura of inevitability or perceived social dominance, but illiberalism is ultimately hollow and vulnerable, especially when it performs poorly,” Cebul told me. He added, “People do not like being governed by crooks and thugs. They want competent governance, not arrogant corruption, and democracy movements can and are winning people over when they call for something better.” ♦

title: “Chronovisor” Captures the Terror of Thinking
author: @NewYorker
content:
In my former life as a Ph.D. candidate in philosophy, I spent a lot of time doing what looked like a lot of nothing. I read; I ruminated; I sat in apparent idleness, unknotting skeins of arguments in my head. At my most gregarious, I talked with other graduate students; we had a habit of contorting our fingers into what those in the business call “philosophy hands,” which at least looked like something, if not exactly like most people’s idea of a meaningful contribution to society. Physicists and chemists could produce pictures of themselves manifestly Doing Science, wearing white coats and wielding pipettes. What did we have to show for ourselves? What did thinking look like, which is another way of wondering, What is thinking, anyway? Is it a substance? A spirit? A shiver?

Whatever it is, it is maddeningly spectral, which is why it was so hard for me to convince anyone (not least my parents and the administrators of my erstwhile university, who refused to provide dental insurance for graduate students until we went on strike) that what I was doing when I was sitting in silence was work, labor in want of compensation or at least dental insurance, alchemy that had the potential to alter the world, however impalpably. The philosopher and critic Elaine Scarry once wrote that “to have great pain is to have certainty; to hear that another person has pain is to have doubt.” We could say almost the same of thinking: from the inside, there is nothing more undeniable (though the thinker may come to doubt her conviction in the face of so much skepticism); from the outside, it is wispier than vapor.

But the difficulty of visualizing thinking hasn’t dissuaded filmmakers from attempting to stage thought’s convolutions onscreen. Cue montages of cryptographers staring at strings of numbers that light up suggestively (the film “A Beautiful Mind”), detectives taking stock of the corpses of murder victims as the camera zooms into the details that strike them as salient (the series “Sherlock”), chess prodigies hallucinating games on the ceiling (the series “The Queen’s Gambit”), and policemen affixing bits of yarn to bulletin boards with thumbtacks (innumerable crime procedurals). In movies and television shows, tortured geniuses think for brief, febrile stretches; then their paroxysms end, and the product of their toil (a cracked code, a jailed murderer, an especially clever checkmate) sets a more readily legible plot into motion. Thought is invariably the handmaiden of action, and the experimental contrivances that dramatize mental exertion—the closeups, the animations, the glowing numbers—are impatiently retired in favor of more standard fare.

“Chronovisor” is one of the few movies about thinking to deviate from this formula. In Jack Auen and Kevin Walker’s mesmerizing directorial début, mental foment is not a prelude to car chases or crime-fighting but an event in its own right. The film has just one character: Béatrice Courte (played by the real-life academic Anne-Laure Sellier), a philosophy professor at Columbia who is hard at work on a monograph about memory. In the opening scene, she describes her project to her peers over drinks in a dark, loud restaurant. She tells them that she is interested in ancient theories of the mind, which hold that different regions of the brain give rise to distinct mental functions—but above all, she continues, she is fascinated by memory palaces. According to the Roman rhetorician Quintilian, Béatrice explains, “an orator wishing to fixate an oration in memory should plan an itinerary through a large imaginary building, all of whose rooms and galleries, courtyards and corridors, statuary and adornments, are as clearly lined out as possible.” Thus a speaker’s roving thoughts are fixed, outfitted with an architecture. But Béatrice’s peers are not interested in memory palaces, and they are not impressed by her fervent monologue: they make their excuses and beg off, leaving her to return home to her desk.

Soon, however, she happens upon an even more ambitious effort to instantiate the insubstantial, to endow memory with form: the chronovisor, a real device that the Benedictine monk Pellegrino Ernetti claimed, in 1972, to have invented. Ernetti hypothesized that events emit electromagnetic waves that linger in the ether, and the chronovisor is intended to record these traces and reconstruct them, creating audiovisual documentation of history, much like a camera shooting a film. “Each one of us gradually leaves behind what happens in a span of seconds, hours, days, months and years, as a visual-acoustic double track,” Ernetti is quoted as saying in one of the sources that Béatrice consults in the course of her manic research. Exploiting this “visual-acoustic double track,” both the real and the filmic Ernetti took what he insisted was a kind of “photograph” of Jesus.

In reality, Ernetti was outed as a fake—the image was revealed to be a doctored reproduction of a sculpture by the Spanish artist Lorenzo Coullaut Valera—but in “Chronovisor” this verdict comes to seem wavering and indeterminate, at least as elusive as the residue of history that he purported to synthesize into images. As Béatrice combs through the archives, always alone, always in the dead of night, always in libraries dense with darkness, she becomes skeptical of the many attempts to discredit the monk and his discovery. “Chronovisor” accelerates and syncopates as she reads on and on—at an ever faster and more scrabbling clip, in increasing desperation—about the Vatican’s determination to silence him and suppress his findings, about threats and subterfuges, about the makings of a great conspiracy. The chronovisor, Ernetti and his supporters claim, was capable of recording not just history but also memories and fantasies, affording whoever controlled it the ultimate means of surveillance. “If I could reach into my heart, take hold of my thoughts, and with my bare hands lay them without further embellishment in your own, then, I confess, the innermost desire of my soul would be fulfilled,” the German Romantic novelist and playwright Heinrich von Kleist wrote, in 1811. Ernetti’s device intrigues and appalls us because it seems to be a means of both satisfying this desire and realizing the fears that it raises: the machine promises, horribly and redemptively, to transmute our inner intangibilities into something that others might see and touch.

Perhaps “Chronovisor” is one of its emanations. The film has the soft, blurred texture of a dream, and it teems not with things themselves but with their echoes. Shadows flit over a curtain in Béatrice’s apartment, and beams cast by a pair of headlights extend into the offing of a road while the car from which they emanate remains out of sight. In place of people’s bodies or faces, we see photographs from the archive and hear voices issuing from offscreen. When Béatrice meets her colleagues at the restaurant, they are positioned behind the camera; in another scene, she delivers a lecture, but the shot conceals her audience, which declines to ask her any questions during the period designated for Q. & A.

What “Chronovisor” captures is not quite the past so much as an oneiric alternative to the present—a place where time detaches from linearity and twines into unrecognizable loops, doubling back on itself. Béatrice is curiously out of synch with the world around her. Night after night, she sits and works. Her life consists of compulsive repetition, of what might even be regarded as a single event: she reads and reads. Her frenzied reading is set outside of time, in an epoch eerily adjacent to our own. Instead of a laptop, she takes notes with a typewriter; instead of searching for references in a digital database, she consults a librarian. All of her sources—books, photographs, magazine articles—are physical, many of them faded with evident age. She uses an iPhone, but only to make calls, never to send texts or summon Ubers or look up directions. She is as much at odds with the norms of her era as she is with the daily rhythms of the city. “Chronovisor” is set almost exclusively at night, when Béatrice sits in gloomy libraries that are otherwise empty, or works in the smudged chiaroscuro solitude of her apartment.

There are many reasons that this ruminative film surpasses previous efforts to portray the vellications of thinking. For one thing, contemplation—not the sheer fact of it but its content—drives the plot. “Chronovisor” makes no capitulations to conventional action; the only drama is the drama of research. (“We view the act of research and scholarship itself as high adventure in its own right,” Auen told an interviewer.) As Béatrice reads, racing toward discovery, we are obliged to read along with her. Passages are limned in white as her gaze passes over them. Sometimes the surrounding text fades away as she homes in on a sentence or phrase. She reads in French, German, and Italian, and the film translates for us in real time, overlaying the words with their English renderings until the pages on the screen become palimpsests. Our eyes move as Béatrice’s do: as she grows hysterical, an enigmatic snippet that she encountered in a book apparently unrelated to Ernetti at the beginning of the film fragments into its rudiments. At first, she reads,

I carefully collected information about those who talked to me; I discovered where they came from and what they wanted to do in life, but I did not know, or trouble to want to know, why they were there. My business was not to think but to listen and above all to look. I was myself a camera. The views of people that I obtained through my own eyes were being recorded elsewhere to make some kind of three-dimensional film whose symbolic significance I would not know until I saw the finished picture. . . . Meanwhile I observed with due photographic care, taking a series of motion pictures. Having recorded my visual observations, I lay down quietly on my bed and died.

Later, each word is isolated in its own shot: “I,” “carefully,” “collected,” “information,” and so on and on. The words flash onto the screen slowly, then accelerate frenetically. “I lay down quietly on my bed and died,” “I lay down quietly on my bed and died,” repeats faster and faster. As Béatrice sits at her desk, phantasmagoric music—selections from Gustav Holst’s orchestral suite “The Planets” and the Gregorian chants that Ernetti studied when he was not too busy inventing occult machines to devote himself to his other interest, musicology—swells and surges. “Chronovisor” is both a patient movie—a steady accretion of atmosphere—and a feverish one. It has the cadence of a burgeoning obsession.

But, above all, it succeeds because Auen and Walker have finally hit on the ideal genre in which to depict the pangs of thinking: horror. At one point, Béatrice listens intently to a 1977 interview with the philosopher Willard Van Orman Quine. The interviewer asks the eminence what he thinks of dualism—the view, hegemonic for much of the history of Western thought, that “there were bodies and there were minds, and that these were two fundamentally different kinds of thing.” Quine rejects dualism on the ground that it cannot explain the mind’s influence on the body, and opts instead for a thoroughgoing physicalism. But Béatrice takes the opposite tack: for her, thought and memory wreak havoc on dualism’s neat dichotomies—and thereby suggest that there is some interstitial entity quivering at the junction of the corporeal and the incorporeal. What is so chilling about this entity is that it always tempts us to suspect that it may not actually exist.

“Chronovisor” is, after all, a chronicle of bruising failures of acknowledgment. Béatrice gives a lecture, and no one asks her any questions; she explains her research to her colleagues, and they leave the restaurant as fast as possible. The academic speaks—and is so resoundingly ignored that she is justified in wondering if she has only imagined it. Most of what happens in “Chronovisor,” like most of what happens when Béatrice is entombed in the library, may or may not have really happened at all, which is another way of saying that “Chronovisor” is a ghost movie, which is another way of saying that it is a film about scholarship. Horror is the ideal genre in which to represent thinking because the true terror of the life of the mind, like the true terror of a haunting, is the sneaking suspicion that nothing is there, that all the agonies of rumination are mere phantoms. Contra Descartes’s famous dictum, to think is to inherit a sliver of the anti-intellectual’s uncertainty—to wonder helplessly if one has in fact accomplished anything at all. I think, therefore I worry that thinking is illusory.

In “Chronovisor,” we eventually come to see some of the images that the device has supposedly recorded—and then we wonder if we are watching a reel of Béatrice’s hallucinations, and then we wonder if the existence of a reel of Béatrice’s hallucinations proves that the chronovisor is real enough to have recorded them. The film is ingeniously ambiguous between these possibilities. But, whether Ernetti’s opus is a momentous innovation or a cheap hoax, whether Béatrice devolves into delusion or comes to see the truth, “Chronovisor” provides what the machine promises, what would be in equal measure harrowing and consoling, what will in any case remain elusive once we leave the cinema and return to the library: proof, for once, that the ghosts are real. ♦

title: “Zombie Bacteria” Might One Day Lurk in the Sewers - Nautilus
content:
Halloween seems like an appropriate time to let you know that zombies are real. Or at least zombie bacteria are, according to a timely new study published in Angewandte Chemie. A team of biologists and nanoscientists made the discovery after researching two species of bacteria used to clean up heavy metals. 

But first, any good zombie story needs a little exposition. Some bacterial colonies can produce a biofilm, a sticky matrix that allows them to adhere to wet surfaces, offers protection, and promotes growth. It’s a little like a slimy neighborhood of bacterial houses (and it also makes up dental plaque). 

Inside the bacterial houses, they’ve got other interesting things going on, like dormant phages. These tiny pieces of viral DNA sit inactive in many bacterial species until certain environmental conditions, like starvation, activate them. By utilizing both these features, scientists from Denmark’s Aarhus University recently discovered something else interesting—bacteria can keep producing DNA after they die.

By starving two different bacterial species (Shewanella oneidensis and Bacillus subtilis) of nutrients , the team activated their dormant phage DNA, kickstarting the replication process and causing the bacteria to burst open. Remarkably, their intracellular “guts” spilled into the biofilm and continued churning out DNA. “In a way, life goes on after the bacterium has died,” study author Gabriel Antonio Minero of Aarhus University said in a statement.

It’s a fascinating finding in its own right, but what’s even more intriguing is how we may be able to harness this pathway for our own benefit. “What matters most to me is that we can hijack the process,” Minero said.

The team coaxed the bacteria into producing DNA folded into specialized structures called G-quadruplexes, which can act like enzymes, binding to other molecules and catalyzing chemical reactions. According to the researchers, that opens up the possibility that the bacteria could be chemically programmed to perform tasks like wastewater cleanup.

In the future, you might sip fresh, pristine water courtesy of zombie bacteria.
